To them, it looks like you ignored them. A contact form that quietly stops delivering loses the warmest leads a business gets, and nothing tells you it happened.

When a domain lapses, the website and the email stop on the same day.

It's one of the easiest things in a business to lose track of. The domain was bought years ago, the renewal notices go to an old address, and the card on file expired. For a .ca, CIRA documents a grace period of up to 45 days, then 30 days of redemption, and after that the name can be released for anyone to register.

Five checks, about five minutes:
Find your registrar on an old receipt.
Look up the expiry date on CIRA's WHOIS page for a .ca, or ICANN's lookup for a .com.
Make sure the registrant is your business.
Turn on auto-renew and update the card.
Turn on registrar lock and two-step verification.

If a letter shows up saying your domain is about to expire, check the company name against your last receipt. A real renewal never asks for your transfer code.

Scared a new website will cost you your Google rankings?

It's the reason plenty of owners stay on a site they've outgrown. The fear is fair, because a careless move breaks every link pointing at the old pages. A careful one follows a map.

List every old page address, starting with the old sitemap and the pages Search Console shows getting clicks. Pair each one with the new page that answers the same question, and set the pair up as a permanent redirect. Test every old address after launch. Then leave the redirects in place, because Google's advice is to keep them for at least a year.

Expect a small dip. Some pages drop a few places for a couple of weeks, then climb back. A top page that loses nearly all its clicks and stays down usually has a missing redirect.
